item.description: arXiv:2602.12090v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantum sensors based on nitrogen vacancy (NV) centers in diamond have been a central topic in the sensing community for more than a decade. item.description: arXiv:2608.09549v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Photoionization induced by trapping and auxiliary laser fields is an inherent feature of many laser-cooling and optical trapping experiments, yet its microscopic dynamics are rarely investigated directly. item.title: Engineering the unknown: building vacuum and cryogenic systems for the quantum frontier
item.description: Qubit decoherence remains the primary barrier to many practical quantum devices. This is why vacuum and cryogenic equipment scaling are key enablers to delivering useful quantum products and systems The post Engineering the unknown: building vacuum and cryogenic systems for the quantum frontier appeared first on Physics World .

item.title: Quantum calculations reveal how spin defects lose energy
item.description: When light hits a tiny defect embedded in a solid material like diamond or silicon carbide, it can kick the defect's electrons into an excited state. These spin defects have the potential to be used as stable, readable qubits for quantum technologies, for example, quantum sensing. But modeling the full physics of their energetics over time—a key step in developing spin defects into new technologies—is a challenging task.

item.description: arXiv:2610.19504v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Magneto-optical traps (MOTs), indispensable to cold-atom-based quantum computing and quantum precision measurement, are increasingly desired in compact and stable form. item.description: arXiv:2610.19511v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ultrafast manipulation of light polarization plays a key role in modern high-speed photonics and optoelectronic operations. item.description: arXiv:2610.19554v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The search for new degrees of freedom (DoF) of light is central to advancing optical information encoding and multiplexing. item.description: arXiv:2610.19964v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Preserving the underlying statistical properties of light during frequency transduction is essential for interfacing spectrally disparate quantum systems. item.title: Photoacoustic-guided reflection-mode wavefront shaping through dynamic biological tissue
item.description: arXiv:2610.20237v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Strong optical scattering limits the depth at which light can be focused and used for imaging in biological tissue. Photoacoustic (PA)-guided wavefront shaping enables non-invasive light focusing in scattering media, but most existing implementations require optical and acoustic access from opposite sides of the sample and a rigidly aligned free-space optical path, which have confined these demonstrations to thin or static samples. item.description: arXiv:2610.20307v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Interlayer excitons (IXs) in transition metal dichalcogenide bilayers possess unique dipolar properties, providing a path for exploring correlated many-body phases, electrically tunable dipole-dipole interactions, and long-range exciton transport. item.title: Software advance brings complex quantum simulations to standard computers
item.description: A major software advance could aid the creation of bigger, more reliable quantum computers, a study suggests. Researchers have developed an algorithm that enables off-the-shelf computers to run quantum simulations previously only possible using the world's most powerful supercomputers.

item.title: Faster molecular simulations identify promising diamond defects for quantum computers and sensors
item.description: A faster way of finding the best diamond-based materials for quantum computers has been developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL). The new approach has already identified promising materials for practical quantum sensors and computers that could one day transform scientific research as a whole. The research was recently published in the journal ACS Central Science and has already garnered attention from other experts in the fiel

item.title: Gravity and quantum information linked through a derivation of Einstein's equations
item.description: Recent research shows that gravity and quantum information are deeply connected and that the shape of spacetime can be traced back to the way information is stored in quantum fields.

item.title: One step closer to quantum computers that can correct their own mistakes
item.description: Researchers from Rutgers, IBM and collaborating institutions have shown that a quantum computer can check what is happening inside it and respond while it is running, repeatedly resetting parts of the system to bring chaotic behavior under control.

item.title: Hybrid quantum computers could finally get to grips with light and matter
item.description: Many of nature's most important processes depend on how particles of matter interact with light and other force-carrying particles. So far, however, it has proven difficult for conventional computers to determine how individual particles behave in these interactions.

item.title: Quantum 'birthmarks' hold lasting traces of a system's past
item.description: Some classical physical systems can explore many configurations over time until their long-term behavior no longer reveals their starting conditions. The sampling of available configurations according to the appropriate statistical distribution is a property called ergodicity.

item.description: Imaginary numbers first appeared in the 16th century as a mathematical invention, introduced to solve equations that real numbers could not. From spin wave to superconducting circuit: A one-way street for quantum information
item.description: Quantum information systems could one day shape everyday life through faster computing, sharper sensing and more secure communication. A new result from the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Argonne National Laboratory and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (U. of I.) marks an important step toward enabling magnetic spins—a quantum property of matter that can be used to store and manipulate information—to play a role in the future of quantum information processing.

item.title: Optical skyrmions can control the motion of magnetic skyrmions
item.description: Magnetic skyrmions (MSks) are swirling patterns of magnetization that form inside certain magnetic materials. They can behave like actual particles in many ways, exhibiting a stable internal structure and distinct boundaries. Because they are extremely small and can be pushed around with relatively little energy, MSks are regarded as promising information carriers in emerging technologies, including low-power memories and logic circuits.
